en: Following that, he states the month and other details for the purpose of the consecration and so forth.
Following that, the months and so forth are taught for the purpose of consecration:
Māgha, Phālguna, likewise Vaiśākha, Śukra, Śuci, and Āṣāḍha— these six months in number are certain to yield exclusively auspicious results.
The four foremost among the planets— Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon—
are renowned as the days that bestow all happiness, affection, and wealth, and are intended for the purpose of consecration.

The months of Caitra, Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādrapada, as well as Āśvina—these six are taught to be the months that bestow the fruit of virtue alone. There are four supreme planets; when the planets Śukra, Bṛhaspati, and Soma are conjoined with these months, [they are most auspicious].
It is taught that all the planets will grant well-being, favor, and wealth; this is for the purpose of consecration.
First is the one known as Khyātā; second, that which is proclaimed as Śubhaphalā; third, from that [comes] Śrīpañcamī; then indeed Daśamī, Saptamī, and Paurṇamāsī.
That which is called Sarvadvidhā is Trayodaśī; it is the all-accomplishing remover of impurities among the seven lunar days (tithis).
The accomplishment of all aims is proclaimed by the sages as the unsurpassed festival of the Buddha’s excellence.

Regarding the second [day] explained first, it is taught as the result of subsequent merit (*anumodana*); that which becomes the third and that which becomes the glorious fifth from that, are certainly the tenth and the seventh. The new moon is the seventh; it is taught that for one who accomplishes everything, strife and sin are destroyed—these are the seven lunar dates.
The Sage has taught that all goals are accomplished through explanation; therefore, one should take joy in the work of a Buddha.
Puṣya, Hastā, Anurādhā, followed by Mṛgaśirā, Rohiṇī, and the latter half of Uttarā; Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Śravaṇa, Bhādrapada, and Āṣāḍha—
these are favorable for growth, and there will certainly be the increase of sons and other blessings, as well as the certain attainment of one's desires in the northern course.
The attainment of knowledge through the hand is not like the appearance of a reflection in a mirror.
In the months of Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada, and Āśvina;

and following those, in the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, Māgha, Phālguna, Caitra, Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada, and Āśvina—during these, one’s children and so forth will increase, and in the month of Māgha, the attainment of one's desires will certainly occur.
On the four fingers, one attains primordial wisdom and gains mastery over space; such is the reality (tathatā) on the hand.

Under Rohiṇī there is an increase of wealth; thereafter, under Mṛgaśiras, there is peace. Under Āṣāḍha, sons live long with manifest and sharp intellects; under Bhādrapada, there is the attainment of success.
Under Puṣya, there is constant victory; under Jyeṣṭhā, one experiences happiness throughout the house; and under Svāti, there is the accomplishment of one's own aims.

In all sacrificial rites involving the entire host of planets, one should act in accordance with the established tradition. [In the *Pūrva-phalgunī* nakṣatra: Wealth increases and there is peace following upon the head. [In *Uttarāṣāḍhā*: For a king, there is long life, sons, brilliant scholars, and intelligence; in the *Śrāvaṇa* month, accomplishments increase. [In *Pūrvā-bhādrapadā*: There is constant victory, happiness, and power; in the *Pūrvā* [nakṣatra], one's goals are fulfilled.
One should perform offerings and sacrifices to all the assemblies of planets that are favorable for the Lhatsam (the junction of the gods) for the accomplishment of bliss.
As soon as it is perfectly accomplished, supreme stability shall arise;
one obtains the sovereignty of a universal monarch—of this there is no doubt.
At the very moment of swift completion, one will abide in the supreme state; there is no doubt that one will attain the sovereignty of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Neither the lunar day, nor the zodiacal mansion, nor even the obstacles and Vināyakas [are hindrances];
all the planets and the deities of the obstacle-mansions are favorable.
There are no lunar days, weekdays, or constellations; there are no obstacles or malevolent spirits either. All obstacles, constellations, deities, and weekdays are in complete harmony.

Thus, although it has been stated in this way, nevertheless, relying upon worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛtti*), everything should be performed at an auspicious moment and so forth, in accordance with the expectations of the world.

Thus, even though it has been taught in that way, one should nevertheless accomplish all things, such as the appropriate times for virtuous practice, in accordance with the agent by relying upon worldly convention.
Alternatively, even during all twelve months, every activity should be performed at auspicious moments and so forth, according to the sequence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Therefore, in all twelve months, all tasks should be carried out according to the sequence of dependent origination, starting with auspicious moments and the like.

Thereafter, when the disciple has requested him two or three times for the purpose of drawing the mandala, if he [the teacher] has not yet gathered the necessary materials, then, having placed the disciple in front of him and visualized a sun-disk with the syllable *hūṃ* at his navel, he should—by means of its rays—expel the sin from the disciple's heart. This sin, produced from the *hūṃ* situated in the heart, is black, deformed, naked, with pendulous testicles, upward-pointing tawny hair, and three feet; having expelled it through the tip of the nose and led that *hūṃ* back into the heart, he should transform it.

Having visualized the great wrathful deity Vajra-hūṃkāra who is about to be described, and having caused him to emerge externally, one should recite: *oṃ sumbha nisumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*; *oṃ gṛhṇa 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*; *oṃ gṛhṇāpaya 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*; *oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vidyārāja amukasya sarvapāpaṃ nāśaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. While reciting this, one should contemplate that the deity, with the blazing vajra held in his hand, renders void the evil that has been expelled.

Thereafter, when the disciple has made the request three times, and if the necessary implements for drawing the mandala have been gathered, at that time the disciple should be placed in front [of the master].

One should meditate on the letter *hūṃ* in the form of a sun disk at its navel; from its light rays, a black, distorted scorpion—naked, with hanging fruit-like testicles, yellow hair bristling upward, and three legs—is drawn out from the letter *kaṃ* located in the heart. Then that *hūṃ* letter also comes to the heart and, through complete transformation, becomes what will be explained.

Having visualized oneself as the great wrathful deity Vajra-hūṃkāra, one emerges [from the heart] and recites: Oṃ sumbha ni sumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ānaya hoḥ bhagavān vidyārāja [Name], sarvapāpān śamaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā |
Reciting this, one should visualize that the blazing vajra held in the hand purifies all sins, rendering them empty.

One should pin down the obstacles to the disciple’s mind with the Amṛtakuṇḍalī mantra in the form of a stake below the navel—reciting "Oṃ vajrakīla kīlayāsya sarvavighnān bandha 2 hūṃ phaṭ" while being commanded by the Vajra-Hūṃkāra himself—and having thus pinned them down, one should burn all the wicked ones with extremely fierce rays from the stake. Then, having visualized that disciple as Samantabhadra through the syllable *saṃ*, one should contemplate a moon disc born from the syllable *a* in his heart, empowered by a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) born from the syllable *aḥ*, for the sake of protection.

Having visualized at the crown of the head a five-pronged vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ* situated upon a moon, its tip pointing upward and its center trampled by Māmakī; and having meditated on all one's limbs being armored by the radiation of subtle yellow vajra-rays produced from the mantra-garland located within the central hub (*varaṭaka*) of the vajra resting on the moon in the heart of the Wisdom Goddess (*jñānadevī*), one should protect oneself while reciting: *oṃ āḥ śaṅkare śāntikare ghuṭa 2 ghuṭṭini ghātaya 2 ghuṭṭini amukaṃ rakṣa svāhā [hūṃ]*. One should also give this *kuṇḍalimantra* to him to recite.

Reciting "Oṃ vajrakīlaya āśā sarvavighnān bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ," one should issue the command with the *hūṃ*-mudrā and strike with the kīla oneself; furthermore, the malevolent beings should be incinerated by the fierce rays of light from the kīla.

That disciple is also visualized in the form of Samantabhadra from the syllable *paṃ*. For the purpose of protection, one meditates on empowering the heart center with a moon mandala arisen from the syllable *āḥ* and a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*) arisen from the syllable *āḥ*. At the head, one visualizes a five-pronged vajra standing upright, arisen from the syllable *hūṃ* situated upon a moon, within the center of which resides Māmaki.

Visualize that from the mantra garland entering the center of the vajra situated upon a moon disk in the heart of that Wisdom Goddess, subtle golden vajra light rays radiate forth, forming a protective armor over the entire body. Then recite: *oṃ āśaṃkare śāntikare ghuta ghuta ghutini ghātaya ghātaya ghūṭani [name] rakṣa svāhā*.
One should perform protection with the mantra recited thus. This [mantra] is also given here for the purpose of reciting the *āvartana* mantra.
When this is done, his obstacles are pacified and his requisites are easily obtained; such is the procedure for gathering disciples.
By acting in this way, one will not be harmed by obstacles and will easily obtain all necessary requisites; such is the ritual for the authentic gathering of disciples.
